title: Improving Vaccines Through Trained Immunity
content: Vaccine development has traditionally focused on optimizing the immunogen, while adjuvants have been used primarily to enhance the magnitude of the adaptive immune response. However, growing evidence that innate immune cells can acquire long-lasting functional changes following stimulation suggests an additional opportunity for vaccine improvement. This phenomenon, known as trained immunity (TRIM), involves metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming of innate immune cells and, in some settings, their bone marrow progenitors. TRIM may provide a mechanistic explanation for the non-specific beneficial effects observed after certain vaccinations, particularly the protection against infections unrelated to the vaccine antigen. Several existing vaccines and adjuvants, including Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG), AS01 and AS03, induce persistent changes in innate immune responsiveness, although these changes do not always conform to classical definitions of TRIM. Experimental studies provide strong mechanistic support for the potential of TRIM to enhance immune protection, but clinical evidence that its induction improves vaccine efficacy remains limited and inconsistent. Importantly, most clinical studies have used TRIM-inducing agents originally developed for other purposes, without systematically optimizing their dose, route of administration or timing, or establishing whether the intended trained phenotype was actually induced. Thus, the potential of deliberately engaging TRIM to improve vaccination remains largely unexplored. In this review, we examine the mechanisms and clinical evidence underlying this approach, discuss the opportunities and limitations of incorporating TRIM inducers into vaccine formulations or administering them separately, and propose experimental and clinical strategies to establish whether controlled induction of TRIM can improve vaccine efficacy.
